# 1.7 Example 6

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

Consider the following passage, asking yourself, **"What is this passage
doing? Is it trying to convince us that something is true?"**

> "Advertisements appear in newspapers, in magazines, on billboards, on
> radio, and on television. A good advertisement should be memorable.
> Don't you agree?"

I don't think that this passage is trying to convince us of anything.
Instead, it's simply telling us things and trusting that we'll accept
them.

"Don't you agree?" might appear to engage us in some critical
reflection, but what if we *don't* agree? Is the passage saying anything
that might *get* us to agree? No. Since this passage is making claims,
*without attempting to establish any of them*, it doesn't contain an
argument.

(It's also useful to note that the passage doesn't contain any inference
indicator expressions, and this is a good reason to at least *suspect*
that the passage doesn't contain an argument. We can't rely on this too
heavily, though, because later on we'll be seeing arguments without
inference indicator expressions.)

## Summary of Example 6

Here's the passage that we considered in this example:

> "Advertisements appear in newspapers, in magazines, on billboards, on
> radio, and on television. A good advertisement should be memorable.
> Don't you agree?"

### Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

We asked, **"What is this passage doing? Is it trying to convince us
that something is true?"** And we decided that it wasn't. There's no
argument here.

Let's see if the next passage contains an argument.
